title: Backtracking, Matrix & Bits
html:
Backtracking, Matrix & Bits

Backtracking

Systematic search: build a candidate incrementally, abandon a branch the moment it cannot lead anywhere, undo, try the next. Depth-first search over a space of decisions.

The skeleton is always the same - choose, recurse, un-choose - and the un-choose is what people forget, leaving state from one branch contaminating the next.

What separates a usable backtracker from an intractable one is pruning: cutting a branch as early as the constraint allows. Placing queens column by column and checking conflicts before recursing is what makes n-queens finish; generating all permutations and filtering them does not.

Handling duplicates is the other recurring difficulty. Sort first, then within a level skip a value equal to the previous one - that skips duplicate branches while still allowing a value to be reused at a deeper level, which "have I used this value" does not.

Costs are exponential by nature: subsets O(2ⁿ), permutations O(n!). Backtracking makes the constant survivable, not the growth.

Matrices

A grid is an implicit graph with four (or eight) neighbours. Flood fill, island counting, shortest path through a maze are graph traversals where the edges are arithmetic.

Practical points:

  • Bounds first. Check the row and column are in range before reading the cell.
  • Direction arrays. [(0,1),(1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0)] and a loop, rather than four copies of the body.
  • Marking visited in place saves O(mn) memory - overwrite the cell, or negate it - at the cost of mutating the caller's data. Fine when documented, a nasty surprise when not.
  • BFS for shortest, DFS for reachability. On a grid, BFS from the start expands in rings, so the first arrival is the shortest.
  • Rotation in place is a transpose followed by reversing each row. Worth knowing because the naive approach needs a second matrix.

Bit manipulation

Integers as sets of flags. Reaches for it when a small collection of yes/no facts must be compact or compared fast.

The operations worth having memorised:

Task Expression
Test bit i (x >> i) & 1
Set bit i x \| (1 << i)
Clear bit i x & ~(1 << i)
Toggle bit i x ^ (1 << i)
Lowest set bit x & -x
Clear lowest set bit x & (x - 1)
Power of two test x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0

x & (x - 1) clearing the lowest set bit is the basis of counting set bits in as many steps as there are bits set, rather than one per bit width.

XOR has two properties that solve a family of problems: x ^ x == 0 and x ^ 0 == x. XOR everything together and values appearing twice cancel, leaving the one that appears once - O(1) space where a set would need O(n).

Subset enumeration: iterate a mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, and bit i says whether element i is in this subset. Compact and fast up to about twenty elements.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to undo state after recursing.
  • Shifting by more than the type's width - undefined or truncated, depending on language.
  • Assuming a right shift on a negative number is logical; in most languages it is arithmetic and keeps the sign.
  • Mutating a grid to mark visited and never mentioning it in the signature or the comment.
  • Mixing up row and column indices; name them row and col, never i and j.
